Every page on LLModel.com: models, providers, comparisons, tools, guides, glossary, videos and more.
A hypothetical AI that can match or exceed people across most cognitive tasks, not just narrow ones.
A model that generates output one token at a time, each conditioned on everything before it.
A model straight out of pretraining that continues text but hasn't been tuned to follow instructions.
A subword tokenization method that builds a vocabulary by repeatedly merging the most frequent adjacent symbol pairs.
A base model further trained to follow instructions and hold a conversation in turns.
k: instruct model instruction-tuned model assistant model

d: The maximum number of tokens a model can consider at once, covering both input and output.
A list of numbers that represents the meaning of a token, sentence or document as a point in space.
Skills that seem to appear suddenly once models pass a certain scale, rather than improving gradually.
A large model trained on broad data that can be adapted to many downstream tasks.
One of the most capable models available at a given time, usually from a well-funded lab.
When a model states something false or unsupported with the same confidence as a fact.
The date after which a model's training data stops, so it knows little about later events.
A neural network trained on huge amounts of text to predict and generate language.
The ability to process very long inputs, from hundreds of thousands to millions of tokens.
Able to take in or produce more than one kind of data, such as text, images and audio.
k: multimodal model multimodal LLM vision-language model

d: A model whose trained parameters are published for anyone to download and run.
The learned numbers inside a model; their count is the usual measure of model size.
An LLM trained to work through a problem in intermediate steps before giving its final answer.
A language model small enough to run cheaply or on a single device, often under about 10B parameters.
Reserved tokens that mark structure, such as the start of a message or the end of output.
The basic unit of text a language model reads and writes, often a word or word fragment.
Splitting text into the tokens a model uses, and mapping each one to an ID number.
The mechanism that lets each token weigh and combine information from other tokens in the sequence.
A transformer made only of decoder layers that predicts the next token from the tokens before it.
k: decoder-only transformer causal language model GPT-style model

d: A model that generates text by refining a whole draft in parallel over several steps, not token by token.
k: diffusion LLM dLLM text diffusion model

d: A transformer component that reads a whole input at once, in both directions, to build representations of it.
k: encoder-only model bidirectional encoder BERT-style model

d: The per-token neural network inside each transformer layer that transforms what attention gathered.
A fast, memory-efficient way to compute exact attention by working in small tiles inside fast GPU memory.
An attention variant where groups of query heads share key and value heads to shrink the KV cache.
Rescaling each token's vector to a consistent range inside every layer, which keeps training numerically stable.
An architecture that routes each token to a few specialist sub-networks, so only part of the model runs per token.
k: MoE sparse mixture of experts sparse MoE

d: Information added to a transformer so it knows the order of tokens, since attention alone ignores order.
A shortcut that adds a layer's input to its output, keeping signals and gradients flowing through deep networks.
A widely used way of encoding token positions by rotating query and key vectors by position-dependent angles.
Attention limited to a fixed number of recent tokens, keeping cost and memory from growing with length.
A function that turns a list of raw scores into probabilities that are positive and sum to one.
A sequence architecture that carries a fixed-size running state instead of attending over every past token.
The neural network design behind nearly all modern LLMs, built around the attention mechanism.
When training on new data makes a model lose skills or knowledge it previously had.
A saved snapshot of a model's weights, and often its training state, at a point in training.
The standard training objective for LLMs, measuring how much probability the model gave the correct next token.
k: loss loss function training loss negative log-likelihood

d: A simpler alternative to RLHF that trains directly on preferred-versus-rejected answer pairs.
Training a smaller student model to imitate a larger teacher model's outputs.
One complete pass of a training process through the entire training dataset.
Further training a pretrained model on a smaller, targeted dataset to change its behavior.
A reinforcement learning method that scores each answer against a group of answers to the same prompt.
Supervised training on instruction-and-response examples so a model learns to follow requests.
The setting that controls how big a step the model's weights take on each training update.
A cheap fine-tuning method that trains small add-on matrices instead of the whole model.
Quality decay when models are trained repeatedly on data generated by earlier models.
When a model learns its training examples too closely and performs worse on new data.
Ways of splitting a model's training or serving across many GPUs so it fits in memory and runs faster.
k: distributed training model parallelism multi-GPU training

d: A family of fine-tuning methods that train a small number of new or selected parameters instead of the whole model.
Everything done to a pretrained model to turn it into a useful, safer assistant.
The first, most expensive training stage, where a model learns language by predicting the next token.
A reinforcement learning algorithm that improves a model in small, controlled steps; the classic RLHF optimizer.
LoRA fine-tuning on top of a 4-bit quantized base model, cutting memory needs dramatically.
